newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Macfarlane takes charge as RBA changes guard.
newsitem.headline: Macfarlane takes charge as RBA changes guard.

text.p: Bernie Fraser walked out the doors of the Reserve Bank of Australia in Sydney's Martin Place for the last time as governor on Tuesday, leaving an institution that has changed markedly under his seven years at the helm.
Those changes will continue under his successor, Ian Macfarlane, following the formalisation with the government of the RBA's inflation objective that Fraser introduced.

Macfarlane, who was one of Fraser's two deputy governors, is seen as an inflation hawk, someone who is prepared to take a hard line to keep inflation low, and for that reason his appointment was well received by markets and analysts.
Under Fraser's tenure, the RBA introduced an informal target of maintaining the underlying inflation rate at an average of two to three percent over the course of a business cycle.
The underlying rate removes volatile and seasonal factors from the consumer price index.

"One of the big successes behind Bernie Fraser was he had that consistent message of underlying inflation, wages and productivity," said Akis Haralabopoulos, chief economist for funds manager GIO Australia.
"That's one reason why he played such an important role in delivering Australia a low inflation environment," he said.

The agreement Macfarlane signed with Treasurer Peter Costello in August committed the RBA to Fraser's informal target, and was seen as enhancing the bank's independence while maintaining the objectives of the RBA's charter.
Those objectives, contained in the Reserve Bank Act, are currency stability, the maintainance of full employment, and economic prosperity and welfare for the nation's people.
Under the agreement, Macfarlane will also appear before a parliamentary hearing twice a year, and release six monthly statements on monetary policy and the outlook for inflation.

Economists said that while Macfarlane may put slightly less emphasis on the RBA's employment objective than Fraser did, it would still be an important consideration, and would not only increase rates.
"He's not someone who's likely to lean on the levers too heavily in either direction," Nomura Research Institute senior economist Andrew Pease said.
"Under Macfarlane there's not going to be very much difference in the way the RBA operates, but there probably will be a slight change in rhetoric," he said.

Some of those perceptions flowed from comments Macfarlane made in May when he said that if an increase in rates to head off inflation resulted in slightly higher unemployment in the short term, that would be a "small price to pay." It would allow the economy to enjoy a longer growth period and push back the chance of a recession.
"In essence, prevention is a lot better than cure," he said.

Macfarlane, who holds a masters degree in economics from Australia's Monash University, worked for the OECD (Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development) in Paris for six years before returning to Australia in 1979.
He joined the RBA in 1979, and in 1988 became head of the economic area. He was appointed Deputy Governor in April 1992.
